title: Phrases and Their Internal Structure
orientation: Phrase analysis explains why a long sentence is more than a chain of neighbouring words. In the new safety report, for example, new modifies safety report while the whole expression can function as a subject, object or another clause element. Identifying those units helps you keep agreement, reference and modifier attachment under control. This lesson gives you a practical way to find heads, group the words that belong together and distinguish a phrase's internal construction from its job in a larger sentence. You will begin with short noun and verb phrases, then examine embedded structures, coordination and the limits of familiar tests such as replacing a group with it. Bracketed analyses make relationships visible without requiring a specialised drawing system. Use several pieces of evidence together: no single substitution or word-order trick can reliably decide every difficult example.
outcomes: Identify the five central phrase classes and their heads.
Distinguish determiners, modifiers and complements inside phrases.
Represent premodification, postmodification, coordination and embedding with clear brackets.
Apply substitution, movement and question-answer diagnostics cautiously.
Explain why phrase class and grammatical function are different descriptions.

modules.title: Heads and the central phrase classes
modules.definition: A phrase is a grammatical unit organised around a head, the element that determines its category and much of its distribution. A phrase may consist of one word or contain several nested units.
foundation: In a familiar noun phrase such as the narrow bridge, bridge is the head. The and narrow depend on that noun, while the complete noun phrase can be used as subject in The narrow bridge needs repairs. The head does not mean the first word or the longest word. It names the organising element. The five phrase classes developed here are noun phrase, verb phrase, adjective phrase, adverb phrase and prepositional phrase. Find the head first, then ask what other material belongs with it. A one-word expression can still occupy a phrase position: in They laughed, they is a noun phrase headed by a pronoun in this course's analysis.
intermediate: A noun phrase is headed by a noun or pronoun; an adjective phrase by an adjective; an adverb phrase by an adverb; and a prepositional phrase by a preposition. Extremely proud of her class is an adjective phrase headed by proud. Very carefully is an adverb phrase headed by carefully. Beside the noticeboard is a prepositional phrase headed by beside, containing the noun phrase the noticeboard as complement. Those labels describe form. A prepositional phrase can function as a modifier inside a noun phrase or as an adjunct in a clause, without changing its phrase category.
advanced: For verb phrases, state the convention being used. The narrow pedagogical convention groups a lexical verb with its auxiliaries: may have been waiting. It excludes an object or location phrase from that particular verb group. A broader syntactic convention includes the lexical verb and its complements inside a VP: read the proposal. Both conventions occur in reputable grammars. This course uses narrow verb group when describing auxiliary order and labels a broader VP explicitly when it includes complements. Do not decide that an analysis is wrong merely because its author has chosen the other stated convention.
expert: A phrase has an external function and internal relations. The entire adjective phrase very proud of her work can be a subject complement, while of her work is an internal complement of proud and very is a degree modifier. A category label does not encode all those functions. Likewise, noun phrases are not restricted to subjects or objects: the following day can function as a time adjunct. A prepositional phrase can also supply a predicative complement, as in the keys are under the mat. These distributions show why adverbial is a function term in this course rather than a universal synonym for adverb phrase.

patterns.form: noun phrase: determiner + modifiers + noun head + post-head material
patterns.meaning: Optional dependents combine around a noun head.

patterns.form: narrow verb group: modal + perfect have + progressive be + passive be + lexical verb
patterns.meaning: Only the selected auxiliary meanings occur; each determines the next verb form.

examples.sentence: Those three unusually steep steps need a handrail.
examples.analysis: Steps heads the subject noun phrase; unusually steep is an embedded adjective phrase.

examples.sentence: The technician may have been waiting outside.
examples.analysis: May have been waiting is the narrow verb group; outside gives additional location information.

examples.sentence: The child seemed surprisingly confident about the interview.
examples.analysis: Surprisingly confident about the interview is an adjective phrase functioning as subject complement.

contrasts.b: The discussion after lunch was brief.
contrasts.note: After lunch is a prepositional phrase in both, but it is a clause adjunct in the first and a noun-phrase modifier in the second.

exceptions: Narrow and broad VP conventions differ; a labelled analysis must make its convention clear.
A noun phrase may contain only a pronoun, as in She arrived, and an adjective phrase may contain only its adjective head.

mistakes.problem: Classification: “at the harbour” is an adverb phrase because it answers where.
mistakes.repair: At the harbour is a prepositional phrase; it may function as a place adjunct.
mistakes.reason: A semantic question suggests function but does not determine phrase class.

mistakes.problem: Classification: the head of “very useful” is very.
mistakes.repair: Useful is the adjective head; very is its degree modifier.
mistakes.reason: The head determines the phrase category rather than merely occupying first position.

glossary.definition: The structural class determined by a phrase’s head.
glossary.example: beside the gate is a prepositional phrase

glossary.definition: A narrow grouping of a main verb and its auxiliaries.

modules.title: Determiners, modifiers and selected complements
modules.definition: A dependent is material associated with a phrase's head. Determiners help establish reference or quantity; modifiers add description; complements are licensed by the head's particular grammatical pattern.
foundation: Look inside a noun phrase before treating every word before its verb as one undifferentiated subject. In these two detailed reports on drainage, these is a determiner, two gives a number, detailed modifies reports, and reports is the noun head. On drainage follows the head and gives its topic. A premodifier occurs before a head; a postmodifier occurs after it. These position labels do not name word classes. A noun can premodify another noun, as in drainage report, while an adjective phrase can appear after a noun, as in the reports available today.
intermediate: A complement is related to a head's lexical pattern, not simply anything standing after it. Proud commonly licenses of her achievement, depend licenses on the grant, and a decision can have an infinitival complement such as to postpone the launch. A modifier adds a description such as the report on the top shelf. Context and grammatical framework can affect the boundary between noun complements and modifiers. For teaching, ask whether the following expression specifies something selected by the head's meaning, such as the content of a claim, or adds an independent property, such as the place of a printed copy.
advanced: Complements are not invariably obligatory. She has already eaten omits the food, although eat also licenses an object in she ate a sandwich. Conversely, the ordinary placing sense of put requires a location or destination expression: she put the tray on the table, rather than she put the tray with no recoverable continuation. Adjunct omission is often a useful first check, but optionality alone is not a complete definition of complement. The same phrase can receive different analyses after different heads: in the library is an optional place adjunct after read but supplies the required location after put the book.
expert: Structure constrains placement. An adjective with a substantial complement commonly follows its noun: students eager to volunteer. Packing the whole sequence before the noun as eager to volunteer students is not the neutral attributive pattern. Modification can also be layered: the very small office near the stairs contains a degree modifier inside the adjective phrase and a location modifier after the noun. A genitive such as the editor's draft can fill a determining role; the apostrophe does not make editor's an adjective by itself. Keep the analyses of grammatical form, internal function and position distinct, especially when comparing school terminology with a more detailed grammar.

patterns.meaning: Position is described relative to the head being modified.
The head’s lexical pattern determines which kinds of complement are possible.

examples.sentence: A detailed report on coastal erosion arrived yesterday.
examples.analysis: Report heads the noun phrase; detailed precedes it and on coastal erosion specifies its topic.

examples.sentence: The students eager to volunteer met after class.
examples.analysis: The complete adjective phrase eager to volunteer follows students.

examples.sentence: She placed the signed form inside the envelope.
examples.analysis: The location completes the placing pattern; its importance comes from the verb’s valency, not from being last.

contrasts.a: She read the book in the library.
contrasts.b: She put the book in the library.
contrasts.note: The same location phrase adds optional circumstances after read but completes the ordinary placing pattern after put.

exceptions: A licensed complement can be omitted in a suitable lexical pattern: she has eaten is complete.
Complement and modifier distinctions may be gradient or framework-dependent, especially inside noun phrases; explain the evidence rather than pretending position settles the issue.

mistakes.problem: They are proud for their daughter’s progress.
mistakes.repair: They are proud of their daughter’s progress.
mistakes.reason: The ordinary adjective-complement pattern is proud of in this meaning.

mistakes.problem: We met a ready to depart group.
mistakes.repair: We met a group ready to depart.
mistakes.reason: The full adjective phrase with its infinitival complement normally follows the noun in this construction.

glossary.definition: The compatibility of a construction with a particular word’s grammatical patterns.

modules.title: Embedding, coordination and structural hierarchy
modules.definition: A hierarchical analysis groups words into units within larger units. Embedding places one unit inside another; coordination links units at a comparable structural level.
foundation: In the cover of the book, the whole expression is a noun phrase headed by cover. Inside it, of the book is a prepositional phrase, and the book is a smaller noun phrase within that phrase. This is embedding. It does not mean that all three units perform the same job. The larger noun phrase may be the subject of a clause, while the smaller one is complement of of. Brackets help you preserve these levels: [NP the cover [PP of [NP the book]]]. Read the structure from the outside inward, then check that every bracket has a matching closing bracket.
intermediate: Coordination links expressions using and, or and related coordinators. The carefully revised draft and the original report coordinates two noun phrases. A phrase can contain coordination internally: the red and blue folders coordinates two adjective modifiers, while the red folders and the blue folders coordinates full noun phrases. These are different structures even if a suitable context lets them refer to the same collection. Shared material can be understood rather than repeated. The editor reviewed and corrected the draft coordinates predicates sharing a subject and object; merely counting occurrences of and does not tell you how many main clauses there are.
advanced: Hierarchy explains attachment ambiguity. The researcher photographed the student with the telescope may describe an instrument used for photographing or identify a student carrying a telescope. One analysis attaches with the telescope to the event; another places it inside the object noun phrase. Both readings follow from available structural relations, not from a defective word ending. If the intended meaning matters, revise explicitly: using a telescope, the researcher photographed the student; or the researcher photographed the student who was carrying a telescope. An interpretation should be supported by context rather than imposed because it was the first one you imagined.
expert: Coordination often links expressions of the same category, but matching category labels is not an absolute condition in every construction. She is a doctor and very experienced can coordinate predicates with different internal categories because both characterise the same subject. Such examples require care with shared grammatical functions. Coordination tests are therefore evidence for constituency, not a proof that any two strings joined by and are interchangeable phrases. In a complete parse, state the relation between each unit and its parent. That approach prevents the common error of treating a noun embedded in an of-phrase as the head governing agreement for the whole subject.

patterns.meaning: A larger noun phrase can contain a prepositional phrase with its own noun phrase.
Coordination can join full noun phrases at the same structural level.

examples.sentence: The manager of the two clinics has resigned.
examples.analysis: Manager heads the complete subject; clinics is embedded as complement of of.

examples.sentence: The red and green indicators were flashing.
examples.analysis: Red and green coordinate within a larger noun phrase headed by indicators.

examples.sentence: The lawyer interviewed the witness with an interpreter.
examples.analysis: The final phrase can describe assistance during the interview; context is needed to exclude other attachments.

contrasts.b: [the cover of the report] and [the revised appendix]
contrasts.note: The first shows embedding within one noun phrase; the second shows coordination of two noun phrases.

exceptions: Different categories can sometimes coordinate when their functions are compatible; identical word-class labels are not an unrestricted universal requirement.
A repeated subject or object may be understood through sharing or ellipsis; analyse the chosen construction before counting clauses.

mistakes.problem: The director of the three museums have replied.
mistakes.repair: The director of the three museums has replied.
mistakes.reason: The larger subject noun phrase is headed by singular director.

mistakes.problem: The analyst compared the budget with the school, meaning the school’s budget.
mistakes.repair: The analyst compared the budget with the school’s budget.
mistakes.reason: Make the intended parallel entities explicit rather than comparing a budget with an institution.

glossary.definition: Inclusion of one grammatical unit inside another.
The structural connection of a modifier to the expression it modifies.
glossary.example: with a torch may modify searching or identify a person

modules.title: Constituency diagnostics and practical parsing
modules.definition: A constituent is a unit within a grammatical structure. Diagnostics such as substitution, movement and answering a focused question can provide evidence about units, but no one diagnostic is decisive in every context.
foundation: Start a parse by finding the finite verb group and the major clause elements, then analyse the phrases inside those elements. In the new assistant filed three invoices, the new assistant is the subject noun phrase and three invoices is the object noun phrase. Replacing the subject with she gives she filed three invoices. This substitution supports the grouping of those subject words. It does not mean that the original phrase was a pronoun or that the replacement has preserved every detail. A diagnostic changes the sentence in order to test one structural possibility.
intermediate: Use more than one check. Ask who filed three invoices; the new assistant forms a natural answer. In the right context, fronting a unit may also be possible: three invoices, the assistant filed before lunch. This marked order supplies evidence for the object grouping, but it is less neutral than the original and may need a contrastive context. Coordination can give further evidence, as in the new assistant and the office manager filed the invoices. A failure under one test can result from meaning, information structure or register rather than proving that the tested string is not a constituent.
advanced: Bracket only what the analysis supports. In a very experienced teacher from Multan, very modifies experienced within an adjective phrase, while from Multan postmodifies teacher in one natural reading. Bracketing [very experienced teacher] as a single adjective phrase misidentifies teacher, the noun head. Likewise, a group of adjacent words may cross a boundary: in she sent the student a note, student a is not a natural constituent merely because the words are neighbours. Avoid constructing a parse solely from translation or a question such as what, which can elicit several kinds of answer.
expert: Substitution tests have restrictions. One can replace some noun-phrase material but does not reproduce every nominal pattern, and it may refer to a different kind of entity from a longer expression. A movement test can change scope or require a special discourse setting. Coordination also has exceptional patterns and shared dependents. Record a tentative analysis when evidence conflicts, then compare a reputable grammar using the same framework. A practical final analysis should name each relevant category, its head and its function in the next larger unit. That is more informative than assigning a label to every individual word while leaving the sentence's larger organisation unexplained.

patterns.form: identify unit → test substitution → check context → compare another diagnostic
patterns.meaning: A sequence of evidence is stronger than a single mechanical trick.
A readable first-pass parse can show major relations before every internal detail is added.

examples.sentence: The revised handbook arrived. → It arrived.
examples.analysis: Pronoun substitution supports treating the revised handbook as a subject noun phrase.

examples.sentence: She spoke very quietly. → How did she speak? Very quietly.
examples.analysis: The manner answer supports the adverb-phrase grouping; quietly is its head.

examples.sentence: We stored the material in the room beside the lift.
examples.analysis: Analyse the room beside the lift as an embedded noun phrase within the in-phrase, rather than treating all location words as one unstructured list.

contrasts.note: The adjective phrase very experienced is internal to the noun phrase in the first and a subject complement in the second.

exceptions: A meaningful answer fragment can identify a phrase in conversation without being a complete formal sentence.
Failure under movement, substitution or coordination alone does not settle every constituency question; contextual and lexical restrictions matter.

mistakes.reason: Teacher is a noun head, so the whole phrase is a noun phrase.

mistakes.problem: The explanation seems quite clearly to the beginners.
mistakes.repair: The explanation seems quite clear to the beginners.
mistakes.reason: The intended subject description takes an adjective phrase headed by clear, not a manner adverb headed by clearly.

glossary.definition: A unit that forms part of a larger grammatical structure.
glossary.example: the revised timetable in We checked the revised timetable

glossary.definition: A test that supplies evidence for an analysis.
glossary.example: Replacing a subject noun phrase with they

questions.prompt: In “the unusually heavy suitcase”, which word is the noun-phrase head?
questions.why: Suitcase determines the category of the whole noun phrase. Heavy heads an embedded adjective phrase; unusually modifies that adjective.

questions.prompt: Using the narrow verb-group convention taught here, identify the verb group in “They might have missed the train”.
questions.why: The narrow group includes the modal, perfect auxiliary and lexical participle; the object is outside this particular grouping.

questions.prompt: What is the phrase class of “under the stairs” in “The cupboard under the stairs is locked”?
questions.why: Under is the preposition head; the whole phrase postmodifies cupboard. Modifier is its function, not its category.

questions.prompt: Which analysis distinguishes class from function correctly?
options: In “the chair beside the window”, beside the window is a prepositional phrase functioning as postmodifier.
Every modifier must be an adjective.
Every word after a noun is its complement.
A phrase answering where must be an adverb phrase.
questions.why: The phrase is headed by beside and modifies chair from a post-head position. The other claims confuse structure with function.

questions.prompt: Which statement avoids treating optionality as the sole complement test?
options: Every optional expression is an adjunct.
A complement is licensed by its head and may be optional in a given lexical pattern.
Anything after a verb is a complement.
questions.why: Eat licenses an object but can occur without one. Licensing and the particular lexical pattern matter alongside omission.

questions.prompt: Complete standard edited agreement: “The label on the three folders ____ unreadable.”
questions.why: The whole subject is headed by singular label. Folders is embedded inside the on-phrase.

questions.prompt: What mainly creates the two familiar readings of “She saw the student with the binoculars”?
options: Different possible attachments of with the binoculars.
questions.why: The phrase can identify the student or describe an instrument used in seeing. Context or explicit restructuring resolves the attachment.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from replacing “the revised timetable” with it in “We checked the revised timetable”?
options: The original expression was one pronoun.
The replacement supports the grouping as a noun phrase in that object position.
Every adjacent string can be replaced with it.
The replacement preserves every detail of the original.
questions.why: Substitution supplies evidence for a grouping and position; it does not change the original words’ categories or preserve all descriptive information.

questions.prompt: Which bracketed analysis locates the adjective phrase correctly?
questions.why: Colleague is a noun head. Very helpful is the adjective phrase modifying it.

questions.prompt: Assess standard edited grammar: (A) The documents on the shelf (B) are ready (C) for collection.
questions.why: Documents is the plural head of the subject noun phrase and agrees with are. The prepositional phrase does not introduce an agreement fault.

questions.prompt: Classify the complete phrase “remarkably slowly” and name its head.
questions.model: It is an adverb phrase headed by slowly; remarkably is a degree modifier.
rubric: Give adverb phrase as the category.
Distinguish head slowly from modifier remarkably.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: In “The answer was quite unexpected”, identify the adjective phrase and its clause function.
questions.model: Quite unexpected is an adjective phrase functioning as subject complement; unexpected is its head.
rubric: Include quite in the adjective phrase.
Name the complement function without calling it an object.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: State the narrow and broad VP groupings for “She has read the report”.
questions.model: The narrow verb group is has read. A broad VP analysis includes has read the report, with the report as the verb’s object complement.
rubric: State which convention each grouping uses.
Include the object only in the specified broad grouping.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Identify the noun phrase in the one-word reply “Who volunteered? — Sam.”
questions.model: Sam is a noun phrase headed by a proper noun, used here as an answer fragment.
rubric: Allow a phrase to consist of one word.
Distinguish an answer fragment from a full declarative sentence.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Parse “these three carefully revised chapters” into determiner, numeral, head and modifying material.
questions.model: These is a determiner; three is a numeral; chapters is the noun head; carefully revised is participial modifying material containing the adverb carefully.
rubric: Identify chapters as the head.
Keep carefully linked to revised rather than to three.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Compare the status of “on the shelf” after put and after read: “She put the book on the shelf”; “She read the book on the shelf”.
questions.model: After put in its placing sense, the location completes the verb’s pattern. After read, a location adjunct is one possible reading; on the shelf can also identify the book as a noun modifier if context supports that reading.
rubric: Recognise the selected location pattern after put.
Acknowledge the attachment ambiguity in the read example.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Arrange “a / proud / of her class / teacher” into a neutral noun phrase that retains all the material.
questions.model: a teacher proud of her class
rubric: Place the full adjective phrase after teacher.
Keep of her class as complement of proud.
alternatives: a teacher who is proud of her class

questions.prompt: Why does “She has eaten” not prove that an object after eat is an adjunct?
questions.model: Eat licenses an object in one pattern but also permits omission of the food. Optionality does not by itself remove the licensed complement relationship in she ate the soup.
rubric: Separate omission from lexical licensing.
Compare the two constructions rather than changing eat’s meaning.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Bracket the nesting in “the key to the cupboard near the lift”, taking near the lift to identify the cupboard.
questions.model: [NP the key [PP to [NP the cupboard [PP near [NP the lift]]]]]
rubric: Embed the cupboard noun phrase inside the to-phrase.
Attach near the lift inside that cupboard phrase.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Contrast “the red and blue files” with “the red files and the blue files” at the level of coordination.
questions.model: The first coordinates adjective modifiers inside a noun phrase. The second coordinates two noun phrases. Context determines whether the two descriptions identify the same set.
rubric: Identify the different coordinated units.
Do not claim that the surface descriptions always have identical reference.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Give two explicit interpretations of “The officer interviewed the witness with a translator”.
questions.model: The officer used a translator while interviewing the witness; or the officer interviewed the witness who was accompanied by a translator.
rubric: Produce an event-related and a witness-identifying interpretation.
Use explicit wording to resolve the attachment.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: In “[NP the roof [PP of [NP the new school]]],” name the head of each noun phrase.
questions.model: Roof heads the outer noun phrase; school heads the embedded noun phrase.
rubric: Identify two different noun-phrase levels.
Do not make school the head of the whole expression.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Use substitution and a focused question to support the grouping “the new laboratory” in “The new laboratory opened yesterday”.
questions.model: It opened yesterday supports the subject grouping. What opened yesterday? — The new laboratory supplies a focused answer identifying the same unit.
rubric: Give a grammatical substitution.
Use the question as additional evidence rather than conclusive proof.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Explain why a movement test should be checked in context.
questions.model: Fronting can require contrast or a particular information structure. A constituent may sound unnatural when fronted in a neutral context even though it is a legitimate unit in the original structure.
rubric: Mention information structure or discourse context.
Avoid treating one failed movement as decisive.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Analyse the class and function of “the following morning” in “We returned the following morning”.
questions.model: It is a noun phrase headed by morning, functioning as a time adjunct.
rubric: Keep noun phrase as the category.
Identify its temporal adjunct function.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Explain why the words “student a” in “She sent the student a note” should not be grouped merely because they are adjacent.
questions.model: They cross a boundary between the recipient noun phrase the student and the direct-object noun phrase a note in the ordinary ditransitive analysis. Adjacency alone is not constituency.
rubric: Locate the boundary between the two objects.
Explain the limitation of an adjacency-only method.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Revise “The plan appears very usefully” to express an evaluation of the plan itself.
rubric: Use an adjective head useful for the subject description.
Keep very as its degree modifier.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Edit while preserving the intended singular head: “The list of rooms on the upper floors are attached. The rooms near the lift is marked in blue.”
questions.model: The list of rooms on the upper floors is attached. The rooms near the lift are marked in blue.
rubric: Make the first verb agree with list.
Make the second verb agree with rooms.
Keep the location modifiers attached to the intended nouns.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: The response seems surprisingly reasonably, meaning that the response is sensible.
rubric: Use an adjective head reasonable as the subject complement.
Retain surprisingly as a degree/evaluative modifier.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: She performed very good during the demonstration.
corrections.model: She performed very well during the demonstration.
rubric: Choose the adverb well for the manner of performing.
Retain the demonstration context.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: We need a capable of handling complaints assistant.
corrections.model: We need an assistant capable of handling complaints.
rubric: Place the full adjective phrase after assistant.
Keep the of + -ing complement.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: The board is aware about the delay. Use the ordinary aware-of pattern.
corrections.model: The board is aware of the delay.
rubric: Use the stipulated aware of complement pattern.
Retain the board’s awareness.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: The owner of the two garages have approved the work.
corrections.model: The owner of the two garages has approved the work.
rubric: Identify owner as singular subject head.
Keep the perfect construction.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: The cupboards beside the stairwell is empty.
corrections.model: The cupboards beside the stairwell are empty.
rubric: Make the verb agree with cupboards.
Do not let singular stairwell determine agreement.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: “The report after lunch was brief.” The writer means the discussion was brief, not the report. Repair the head choice.
corrections.model: The discussion after lunch was brief.
rubric: Use discussion as the intended noun head.
Retain the time modifier and the evaluation.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: “The people upstairs are waiting.” Does standard grammar require upstairs to be changed?
corrections.model: No change is required. Upstairs can postmodify people here and identify their location.
rubric: Accept the original grammatical construction.
Do not require every noun modifier to be an adjective.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

transformations.prompt: Remove the ambiguity by making the telescope an instrument used by the photographer: “The photographer observed the traveller with a telescope.”
transformations.model: Using a telescope, the photographer observed the traveller.
rubric: Attach the instrument to the observing event.
Keep photographer as the understood user of the telescope.
alternatives: The photographer used a telescope to observe the traveller.

transformations.prompt: Turn “The volunteers were eager to help. The coordinator welcomed them.” into one sentence with a postmodified object noun phrase.
transformations.model: The coordinator welcomed the volunteers, all eager to help.
rubric: Preserve eagerness of the entire original volunteer group.
Use a supplement rather than silently restricting the group to an eager subset.
alternatives: The coordinator welcomed the volunteers who were eager to help. (A relative-clause postmodifier.)

writing.prompt: Write an 80–110-word description of a workplace or study space. Include one complex subject noun phrase, an adjective phrase with a complement, an adverb phrase and a prepositional phrase modifying a noun. Add a bracketed analysis of one sentence.
writing.model:
The study room beside the old courtyard opens at nine each morning. Its narrow windows admit enough light for reading, and the large table near the door holds reference books. Several students eager to prepare together meet there after lunch. They work remarkably quietly until the afternoon break, although the adjoining corridor becomes noisy when classes finish. A notice on the inner wall explains how visitors can reserve the room. The room also contains a small cupboard for shared stationery, which the caretaker checks at the end of each week.

Analysis: [NP The study room [PP beside [NP the old courtyard]]] [verb group opens] [time adjunct at nine each morning]. Eager to prepare together is an adjective phrase; remarkably quietly is an adverb phrase.
rubric: Use and identify all four required phrase structures.
Separate phrase category from its grammatical function.
Make the bracketed analysis consistent with the sentence.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 1: identify word class and function of quiet in “The office is quiet”.
recall.model: Quiet is an adjective functioning as subject complement.
rubric: Keep category and function separate.
Do not label quiet an object.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 11: distinguish “hard work” from “work hard” structurally.
recall.model: In hard work, hard is an adjective modifying the noun work. In work hard, work is a verb and hard is an adverb modifying it.
rubric: Identify the class of work in both patterns.
Identify the modifier’s corresponding category and function.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 10: “The quality of the samples were inconsistent.”

rubric: Identify quality as the singular subject head.
Retain the complement inconsistent.
